node.label: Philip Curtin
node.date_label: The Image of Africa (1964) · The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969) · Cross-Cultural Trade in World History (1984) · On the Fringes of History: A Memoir (2005)
node.description: A historian of Africa, forced migration and cross-cultural connections who combined quantitative reconstruction with comparative world history. Joseph C. Miller’s substantive memorial describes how the slave-trade census grew from a question about regional economic context and how its estimate prompted further archival work. The same account identifies recurring global subjects such as trade, plantations, migration and disease. The entry preserves uncertainty and the distinction between counting a forced migration and explaining enslaved people’s lived experience; it does not adopt a historical estimate as a current audited total.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Image of Africa (1964); The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969); Cross-Cultural Trade in World History (1984); On the Fringes of History: A Memoir (2005).
node.scope_note: Existing philip_curtin profile reused. New arguments use named substantive reader Miller; the books remain unread and numerical estimates are not freshly certified. The earlier Hodgson/editor-preface bibliography remains limited to its own scope and supplies no new influence claim. The 1964/1965 discrepancy is explicit, and the contemporary bibliography supports 1964.

incident_edges.relationship: Curtin’s census contributes quantitative reconstruction of the slave trade
incident_edges.evidence_note: Curtin’s book replaces Gilroy as the reference. Its estimates were subsequently revised; quantitative inquiry did not begin or end with this book. The current Curtin check is bibliographic; numerical series and the later 1999 database still require separate review.

incident_edges.relationship: Makes source criticism and estimation central to reconstructing the scale of the Atlantic slave trade.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Joseph C. Miller’s 2009 account of the census’s origin, uncertainty and later archival responses. No fresh reading of the census or audit of modern SlaveVoyages totals; counting is not a substitute for enslaved experience.

incident_edges.relationship: Develops comparative questions around recurring cross-cultural trade, migration, plantations and disease.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Miller’s substantive account supplies the methodological characterization; the publisher record supports title/date only. A specific comparative agenda, not the claim that one historian founded all global history or a causal affiliation arrow.

incident_edges.relationship: Iriye invokes Curtin’s warning against self-knowledge alone when arguing that historians should communicate across cultural boundaries.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Specific methodological use, not career lineage. Curtin’s original address remains unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Curtin’s discussion of the expanding meanings of creole before specifying his own Atlantic-creole terminology.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own selected digital PartI note1 explicitly quotes and attributes Curtin Economic Change in Precolonial Africa1975 pp138–139n5, then warns that creole has no universally accepted usage and states his own definitions. This is bounded conceptual use from an authorial note, not a general genealogy or direct reading of Curtin’s complete book; cited original and continuous Berlin chapter unread.
